title: Extensibility & foreign code — where it stands
eyebrow: Capability positioning · read from the source, not from memory
thesis: The most honestly-mixed group in the survey. What ships is real but modest: Softanza consumes a large, carefully-vendored foreign-code stack (tree-sitter, SQLite, curl, mbedTLS, zlib, ggml, RmlUi, HarfBuzz, PCRE2… all compiled from source, no external runtime deps) — genuinely strong foreign-code integration — plus pragmatic interop: subprocess bridges that run Python/R/Julia/C/Prolog/Node, Ring shims that let you paste Python/PHP/SQL, and tool bridges to Graphviz/QML. But the actual extensibility story the group is named for is overwhelmingly planned: there is no in-process FFI, no embedded interpreter, and the plugin plane ("a plugin is governed foreign capability — accept code you don't trust, audit what it did, undo it") is a detailed plan with a recovered reference archive but zero live code.
grid_title: Twelve lanes, each against its category leader
grid_lede: Every lane names what actually ships, the tools it is fair to measure against, and the one thing still owed. The split runs down the middle: Softanza using foreign code is real; letting a user plug in foreign code is mostly designed, not built.

lanes.engine: A large, disciplined vendored C/C++ stack compiled into the engine from source via Zig — tree-sitter, SQLite, curl, mbedTLS, zlib, ggml, RmlUi, GLFW, wgpu, HarfBuzz, SheenBidi, PCRE2, utf8proc, Snowball, AccessKit — with no external runtime dependencies (each vendored, pinned, and patched where needed).
lanes.owed: Foreign-code integration is genuinely strong — a dozen serious native libraries built and linked cleanly. This is the one lane where "foreign code" is a shipped strength, not a plan.

lanes.engine: `stz_polyglot` parses Python and JavaScript source (vendored tree-sitter grammars, compiled — no interpreter) into a shared declaration/call protocol that feeds `stzCodeGraph` — understanding foreign code without running it.
lanes.owed: Two grammars, parse-only (see the Metaprogramming page for the deep rating). It reads foreign code; it does not execute it.

lanes.engine: Subprocess bridges to external tools: `stzDotCode` (Graphviz `dot` → SVG/PNG), `stzQmlCode` (Qt's standalone `qml` runtime), and `stzImgToAscii` (a vendored `im2ansi.exe`) — same write-temp / spawn / read shape.
lanes.owed: Real, loaded bridges (dot, qml) — though `stzImgToAscii` ships but is never loaded, and each depends on the external tool being installed.

lanes.engine: `stzExterCode` + wrappers run Python, R, Julia, C, Prolog and Node: write the snippet to a temp file, wrap it with a result-serialization prelude, shell out via `stzSystemCall`, and `eval()` the transformed result back into a Ring value.
lanes.owed: Subprocess-only — high overhead, no shared memory, gated on installed toolchains and hardcoded `d:\` paths — and the whole suite is currently red (lane 12). It runs foreign code, but coarsely.

lanes.engine: Ring shims so you can paste foreign syntax and run it as Ring with small edits: Python (`range`/`print`/f-strings), PHP, C#, Perl, C ternaries, and the biggest — SQL-in-Ring (`SELECT/FROM_/WHERE_/ORDER_BY` as functions over `stzTable`).
lanes.owed: A distinctive paste-and-tweak ergonomic — but these are shims, not a runtime (no foreign interpreter), coverage is thin (the JS shim is an empty stub), and the suite is red (lane 12).

lanes.engine: Both shipped interop modules have real test suites with genuine assertions (language-table checks, `iif`/`range` comparisons, port examples with expected outputs).
lanes.owed: The suites are entirely red: `C22 function-redefinition`, 0 passing — the base library loads fine, so it's a duplicate definition in the shims (e.g. `echo`/`range0` defined in both the PHP and Python files, both loaded). Shipped, but not currently trustworthy.

lanes.engine: None for user code. There is no `dlopen` / `cffi` / direct-C-call surface — (`extern` in the engine is only vendored C headers the engine itself links).
lanes.owed: No way for a user to call a C function directly and fast. The only "call out" is the subprocess bridge (lane 4) — an order of magnitude heavier than FFI.

lanes.engine: None. No in-process Python / JS / Lua interpreter embedded in the engine; foreign execution is subprocess-only.
lanes.owed: No embedded runtime means no fast, in-memory foreign execution and no shared data structures across the language boundary — the Pyodide/embedded-VM model is entirely absent.

lanes.engine: A detailed plan of record (PL0–PL5) and a `recovered/` archive — a working single-file 2024 system and a never-run 2025 refactor, both explicitly "reference only, not loaded." The enabling VM primitives (`ring_state_*`) exist. No live plugin code; not loaded in `stzBase`; no test dir.
lanes.owed: The group's named headline is unbuilt — the recovered 2024 system proves the mechanism works (~3.1 ms/call, per-call VM-state isolation), so PL1 is a rebuild on a known-good base, not a discovery.

lanes.engine: The distinctive thesis, designed: a five-clause contract — isolation, per-call ledger, cooperative constraint, currency (fswatch + hash), and governance (trust posture picks the isolation tier; verdicts to `stzRuleReport`), with reversible updates (`XfU`) and `@plugin_author` provenance.
lanes.owed: "Accept capability you don't trust — from humans or models — and prove afterwards what it did, and undo it." A genuinely distinctive idea (per-call audit + effect reversal + provenance) — but entirely unbuilt.

lanes.engine: Designed two-tier isolation (`:State` in-process `ring_state` / `:Process` reactor spawn), with the host-state guarantee "by physics" (a VM state can't reference host memory). Explicitly refuses to be a security sandbox — governance, not syscall confinement.
lanes.owed: Unbuilt, and by design it is not a syscall-level sandbox — a plugin in the process tier can still do what the process can. Honest, but a real boundary vs WASM/V8 isolation.

lanes.engine: None — and the plugin plan explicitly states it is not a package manager, marketplace or code-signing scheme.
lanes.owed: No discovery, versioning, dependency resolution or signed distribution — deliberately deferred. Even a manifest + provenance story would be a first step the plan reserves for later.

gaps_title: The gaps, ordered by return — not by size
gaps_lede: Three tiers. The first is a cheap correctness fix plus the group's headline plane; the second is the fast interop path and finishing the shipped bridges; the third is the embedded/distribution reach.

tiers.title: Tier A — fix what's red, build what's named

items.title: Fix the red interop suites
items.text: extercode and extincode ship and load, but 0 tests pass — a `C22` duplicate-definition (the shims define `echo`/`range0` in both the PHP and Python files). Namespace the shim functions so the two shipped modules become trustworthy. Cheap, and it turns "shipped-but-red" into "shipped."

items.title: Build the plugin plane (PL0–PL5)
items.text: The group's named headline — governed foreign capability — with a working recovered reference and the enabling `ring_state_*` primitives already in the VM. PL1 rebuilds on a known-good base; the whole point (audit + reverse untrusted capability) has no competitor.

tiers.title: Tier B — the fast path & finish the shipped bits

items.title: In-process FFI
items.text: A `dlopen`/cffi-style bridge so a user can call a C function directly — the fast, shared-memory path the subprocess bridge (lane 4) can never be. It also underpins any future embedded-interpreter work.

items.title: Configurable toolchain discovery
items.text: Retire extercode's hardcoded `d:\` interpreter paths for real discovery (PATH / config), so "run this Python" works on a machine that isn't the dev box.

items.title: Wire the plugin isolation tiers
items.text: The `:State` (`ring_state`) and `:Process` (reactor spawn) tiers the plan designs — the mechanical half of the plugin plane, on which the governance clauses hang.

items.title: The governance / audit / reversal contract
items.text: The plan's crown: per-call ledger, `XfU` effect reversal, provenance, and verdicts into the one CI gate — the "prove what it did and undo it" guarantee that distinguishes this plane from every mainstream plugin system.

items.title: Embedded interpreters
items.text: An in-process Python or Lua (Pyodide-style) for fast foreign execution with shared data — the heavy alternative to subprocess interop, worth it where the round-trip cost dominates.

items.title: A manifest & provenance layer
items.text: Not a marketplace (deliberately out of scope) — but a plugin manifest, versioning and signed provenance, the minimum a governed-capability plane needs to trust where a plugin came from.

notes.lead: The honesty line on the ratings.
notes.text: Re-surveyed from `main` — and it corrected an earlier read: `extercode` and `extincode` are not plan-only; they ship and are loaded. But three caveats hold: (1) both shipped interop suites are entirely red (`C22` function-redefinition, 0 passing — a duplicate-def in the shims, not a base-library fault); (2) the `plugin` plane is genuinely plan-only (no live code, not loaded, no test dir), with a recovered archive marked "reference only"; (3) there is no in-process FFI or embedded interpreter anywhere — foreign execution is subprocess-only. The "governed foreign capability" thesis is distinctive and its VM primitives exist, but it is unbuilt.

Softanza is strong at using foreign code (a serious vendored native stack) and pragmatic at bridging to it (subprocess interpreters, syntax shims, tool shells) — but the extensibility it is named for, letting a user or a model plug in code the host governs, audits and can undo, is a compelling design with no shipped implementation, and the interop that does ship needs its test suites made green.

footer: Read from the source on 2026-09-16, from a read-only `main` worktree — Ring faces under `base/extercode` (`stzExterCode`, `stzPythonCode/RCode/JuliaCode/PrologCode`, `stzDotCode`, `stzQmlCode`) and `base/extincode` (`stzExtinPython/Php/Sql/C/CSharp/Perl`), both loaded in `stzBase.ring`; `base/plugin` = plan (`SOFTANZA_PLUGIN_PLAN.md`, `…_COMPARATIVE_STUDY.md`) + a `recovered/` archive, not loaded; consumption via the engine's vendored stack (tree-sitter, SQLite, curl, mbedTLS, zlib, ggml…); VM primitives `ring_state_*`; guards under `test/extercode` + `test/extincode` (present, currently red), `test/plugin` absent. Ratings reflect what the guards prove.
